source_text: Sed non primum - inquit - quod spiritale est, sed quod animale; deinde, quod spiritale est. Primus homo de terra, terrestris; secundus homo de caelo, caelestis; sicut portavimus imaginem terrestris, portemus et imaginem illius caelestis [n234] . Aperte nempe transit ad studia, vultque tantum interesse inter praeteritam nostram et praesentem conversationem, quantum interest inter mortalitatem et immortalitatem. Primus - inquit - homo de terra, terrestris; secundus homo de caelo, caelestis; nomine substantiarum propositi indicat diversitatem. Neque enim Christus, quem hominem caelestem vocat, carnem suam de caelo deposuit, quam de semine David, de semine Adam, et intra mulierem de mulieris carne suscepit. Terrestrem ergo et caelestem refert ad virtutes et vitia. Denique sequitur: Sicut portavimus imaginem terrestris; portemus etiam imaginem illius caelestis. Sic et ad Romanos: Humanum est quod dico, propter infirmitatem carnis vestrae; sicut enim exhibuistis membra vestra servire immunditiae, et iniquitati ad iniquitatem; ita nunc exhibete membra vestra servire iustitiae in sanctificationem [n235] . Tenorem vero sequens exhortationis assumptae, subdit, quod nisi intellegatur, omnia eius videbitur dicta subruere: Hoc ergo dico, fratres, quia caro et sanguis regnum Dei possidere non possunt, nec perpetuitatem interitus possidebit. Nempe in his locis, in quibus nihil aliud quam de affirmanda carnis resurrectione laboraverat, quam dixerat in regni gloria collocandam, nunc pronuntiat: quia caro et sanguis regnum Dei possidere non possunt. Si caro non possidet, si sanguis non possidet, ubi est, cuius supra pompam regenerat resurrectio mortuorum? Verum Scripturae more, carnem et sanguinem, vitia, non substantiam nominavit. Denique hoc idem aperuit: Ecce mysterium vobis dico: omnes quidem resurgemus, sed non omnes immutabimur. Intellexit se magister egregius, supra beatitudini tantum futurae resurrectionis vocabulum vindicasse; et ideo illud ne ambiguum remaneret, absolvit: Omnes quidem, resurgemus; ecce quae est excitatio communis: sed non omnes immutabimur; ecce ubi est resurrectio beatorum. Immutatio ergo in gloriam illis tantum debetur, qui non iram Dei, sed amorem merentur. In momento - inquit - in ictu oculorum, in novissima tuba, et mortui resurgent incorrupti, et nos immutabimur. Denuo hic transit ad eos sanctos, quos dies ille in carne reperiet; et dicit quoniam in momento tam brevi, quam potest esse extremus finis sonorum, et qui mortui fuerant, excitentur incorrupti, id est, integri; et qui inventi fuerint, immutentur in gloriam. Oportet enim hoc corruptibile induere incorruptelam; et mortale hoc induere immortalitatem. Cum autem mortale hoc induerit immortalitatem, tunc fiet sermo qui scriptus est: Absorpta est mors in victoriam tuam. Ubi est, mors, tuus aculeus? Ubi est victoria tua? Aculeus autem mortis, peccatum; virtus autem peccati, lex [n236] . Ostendit, ut saepe, quoniam de sanctorum tantum resurrectione loqueretur; ideo praetermittens illam impiorum excitationem, dignum esse pronuntiat ut in corporibus sanctorum corruptibilitas aeternitate gloriae devoretur. Cum autem hoc, inquit, fuerit impletum, tunc licebit insultare diabolo, et morti perpetuae, quae hanc corruptionem naturalem fecerat malam videri; tunc increpabunt sanctorum gaudia, contusum a se aculeum mortis videntium, dicentque: Ubi est, mors, aculeus tuus? Ubi est victoria tua? Aculeus autem mortis, peccatum; virtus autem peccati, lex. Id est: O tu mors aeterna, aculeum habebas peccatum, quo desertores iustitiae vulnerares; quoniam si hoc aculeo armata non esses, id est, peccato voluntario, nulli omnino nocuisses. Peccatum hoc et hunc aculeum viribus fidei confractum vides, remuneratione nostra teste, a qua nos conabaris abducere; aculeus quippe tuus peccatum fuit, et virtus peccati tui lex erat; quoniam ubi non est lex, nec praevaricatio [n237] . Vel certe quamvis aculeus tuus peccatum esset; tamen fortior factus est apud praevaricatorum dumtaxat animos, postquam mors ei legis admota est; quae tamen non ad hoc data fuerat, ut acueret. Lex enim sancta, et mandatum sanctum, et iustum et bonum; sed peccatum ut appareat peccatum, per bonum mihi mortem operabatur, ut fieret supra modum ipsum peccatum peccans per mandatum [n238] . Haec ergo virtus, quam aculeus tuus spontaneae in nobis iniquitatis consequebatur adiutu, fidelium virtutibus, fidelium iam coronis victa comprobatur, et fracta. Insultamus igitur tibi: Deo nostro gratias referentes, qui dedit nobis hanc victoriam per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum [n239] .
pass_a_gloss: But not first, he says, what is spiritual, but what is animal; then, what is spiritual. The first human from earth, earthly; the second human from heaven, heavenly; as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of that heavenly. Openly indeed he passes to studies, and wants there to be as much difference between our past and present conversation, as there is between mortality and immortality. The first, he says, human from earth, earthly; the second human from heaven, heavenly; by the name of substances he indicates a diversity of purpose. For neither did Christ, whom he calls a heavenly human, put down his flesh from heaven, which he took up from the seed of David, from the seed of Adam, and within a woman from a woman's flesh. He therefore refers earthly and heavenly to virtues and vices. Finally it follows: As we have borne the image of the earthly; let us also bear the image of that heavenly. Thus also to the Romans: It is human what I say, on account of the infirmity of your flesh; for as you exhibited your members to serve uncleanness, and iniquity unto iniquity; so now exhibit your members to serve justice unto sanctification. But following the tenor of the exhortation taken up, he subjoins, which unless it is understood, he will seem to undermine all his sayings: This therefore I say, brothers, that flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, nor will perpetuity possess destruction. Indeed in these places, in which he had labored nothing other than for affirming a resurrection of the flesh, which he had said must be placed in the glory of the kingdom, he now pronounces: that flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God. If flesh does not possess, if blood does not possess, where is that whose pomp above a resurrection of the dead regenerates? But by the custom of Scripture, he named flesh and blood vices, not substance. Finally he opened this same: Behold I say a mystery to you: we will all indeed rise, but we will not all be changed. The outstanding teacher understood himself, above to have claimed the word of resurrection for future blessedness only; and therefore lest that remain ambiguous, he finished: We will all indeed rise; behold what the common excitation is: but we will not all be changed; behold where the resurrection of the blessed is. A change therefore into glory is owed only to those who deserve not God's wrath, but love. In a moment, he says, in the twinkling of eyes, at the last trumpet, and the dead will rise incorrupt, and we will be changed. Again here he passes to those holy, whom that day will find in the flesh; and he says that in a moment so brief as the extreme end of sounds can be, both those who had been dead may be stirred incorrupt, that is, intact; and those who shall have been found may be changed into glory. For this corruptible must put on incorruption; and this mortal put on immortality. But when this mortal shall have put on immortality, then will be done the speech which is written: Death is swallowed in your victory. Where is, death, your sting? Where is your victory? But the sting of death, sin; but the virtue of sin, the law. He showed, as often, that he was speaking only about a resurrection of the holy; therefore omitting that excitation of the impious, he pronounces it worthy that in the bodies of the holy corruptibility be devoured by an eternity of glory. But when this, he says, shall have been fulfilled, then it will be allowed to insult the devil, and perpetual death, which had made this natural corruption seem evil; then the joys of the holy will chide, seeing the sting of death bruised by themselves, and they will say: Where is, death, your sting? Where is your victory? But the sting of death, sin; but the virtue of sin, the law. That is: O you eternal death, you had sin as a sting, by which you would wound deserters of justice; because if you had not been armed with this sting, that is, with voluntary sin, you would have harmed no one at all. You see this sin and this sting broken by the powers of faith, our remuneration being witness, from which you were trying to lead us away; for your sting was sin, and the virtue of your sin was the law; because where there is not a law, neither is there prevarication. Or certainly although your sting was sin; nevertheless it was made stronger among the minds of prevaricators at least, after a death of the law was applied to it; which nevertheless had not been given for this, that it would sharpen. For the law is holy, and the mandate holy, and just and good; but sin that it may appear sin, was working death for me through the good, that sin itself sinning through the mandate might become above measure. This virtue therefore, which your sting of a spontaneous iniquity in us was obtaining by help, is proved already conquered and broken by the virtues of the faithful, by the crowns of the faithful. We therefore insult you: rendering thanks to our God, who gave us this victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

pass_b_english: ‘But the spiritual did not come first,’ he says; ‘the animate came first, and then the spiritual. The first human is from earth, earthly; the second human from heaven, heavenly. As we have borne the earthly one’s image, let us also bear the heavenly one’s image’ (1 Corinthians 15:46–47, 49). He plainly turns to our pursuits, wanting the difference between our past and present conduct to be as great as that between mortality and immortality. ‘The first human is from earth, earthly; the second human from heaven, heavenly.’ He uses the names of substances to indicate a difference of purpose.

Christ, whom he calls the heavenly human, did not bring his flesh down from heaven. He received it from David’s seed, from Adam’s seed, and within a woman from a woman’s flesh. ‘Earthly’ and ‘heavenly’ therefore refer to virtues and vices. The next words confirm it: ‘As we have borne the earthly one’s image, let us also bear the heavenly one’s image.’ So also to the Romans: ‘I speak in human terms because of your flesh’s weakness. Just as you presented your members to serve uncleanness and lawlessness toward lawlessness, now present your members to serve justice toward sanctification’ (Romans 6:19).

Following the course of his exhortation, he adds something that, unless understood, will seem to overthrow all he has said: ‘I say this, brothers: flesh and blood cannot possess God’s kingdom, nor will decay possess everlasting life’ (1 Corinthians 15:50). In these very passages he has labored only to establish flesh’s resurrection, saying it would be placed in the kingdom’s glory. Now he pronounces that flesh and blood cannot possess God’s kingdom. If flesh cannot possess it and blood cannot possess it, where is the resurrection of the dead whose splendor he has been setting forth above? But, following Scripture’s usage, he calls vices, not substance, ‘flesh and blood.’

He makes this very point clear: ‘Look, I tell you a mystery: we shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed’ (1 Corinthians 15:51). The outstanding teacher understood that above he had reserved the word resurrection for future blessedness alone. Therefore, to remove ambiguity, he explains: ‘We shall all rise’—here is the common raising; ‘but we shall not all be changed’—here is the blessed’s resurrection. Change into glory is owed only to those who deserve God’s love rather than his anger.

‘In a moment,’ he says, ‘in the blink of an eye, at the last trumpet, the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed’ (1 Corinthians 15:52). Here again he turns to the saints whom that day will find in the flesh. He says that in a moment as brief as the final ending of a sound, those who had died will be raised incorruptible—that is, whole—and those found alive will be changed into glory.

‘For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal put on immortality. When this mortal has put on immortality, then the written saying will happen: Death has been swallowed up into your victory. Where, death, is your sting? Where is your victory? Death’s sting is sin, and sin’s power is the law’ (1 Corinthians 15:53–56; compare Isaiah 25:8; Hosea 13:14).

He shows, as often, that he speaks only of the saints’ resurrection. Passing over the ungodly’s raising, he pronounces it fitting that in the saints’ bodies corruptibility should be swallowed by everlasting glory. When this is fulfilled, he says, it will be possible to taunt the devil and perpetual death, which made this natural corruption seem evil. Then the saints’ joys will rebuke it, seeing that they have crushed death’s sting, and will say: ‘Where, death, is your sting? Where is your victory? Death’s sting is sin, and sin’s power is the law.’

That is: Eternal death, you had sin as a sting with which to wound deserters of justice. Had you not been armed with this sting—that is, voluntary sin—you would have harmed no one at all. You see this sin and this sting broken by faith’s strength. Our reward bears witness, the reward from which you tried to lead us away. Your sting was sin, and the power of your sin was the law, because ‘where there is no law, neither is there transgression’ (Romans 4:15).

Or, certainly, although sin was your sting, it became stronger—only in transgressors’ minds—after the death threatened by the law was brought to it. Yet the law was not given to sharpen it. ‘The law is holy, and the commandment holy, just, and good. But sin, to appear sin, produced death in me through the good, so that sin itself might become exceedingly sinful through the commandment’ (Romans 7:12–13).

This strength your sting gained through the assistance of our voluntary iniquity is now proved defeated and broken by believers’ virtues and believers’ crowns. We therefore taunt you, ‘giving thanks to our God, who gave us this victory through our Lord Jesus Christ’ (1 Corinthians 15:57).
